title: Staging Precisely: Small, Reviewable Commits
intro: You fixed a bug, renamed a variable, and left a debug print in, all in one file. 'git add .' would commit the lot as one unreadable change. The staging area exists so you can decide what goes into each commit.

steps.prompt: Stage only some of the changes in your working tree, choosing hunk by hunk.
steps.fake_output:
@@ -41,7 +41,7 @@ def charge(order):
-    total = order.amount
+    total = order.amount_cents
(1/3) Stage this hunk [y,n,q,a,d,s,e,?]? y
@@ -58,6 +58,7 @@ def charge(order):
+    print("DEBUG", order)
(2/3) Stage this hunk [y,n,q,a,d,s,e,?]? n
steps.explanation: The bug fix is staged; the debug print is not.
steps.why: 'add -p' makes you read your own change before committing it, which catches debug lines and accidental edits. 's' splits a hunk that's too big, and 'e' lets you edit it by hand. It beats 'git add .' for anything you'll want to review or revert later.

steps.prompt: Review exactly what will go into the commit (the staged changes only).
steps.fake_output:
@@ -41,7 +41,7 @@ def charge(order):
-    total = order.amount
+    total = order.amount_cents
steps.explanation: Only the one-line fix is staged.
steps.why: Plain 'git diff' shows what is NOT staged yet; '--staged' shows what the commit will contain. Checking --staged right before committing is the cheapest code review there is.

steps.prompt: You staged config/local.yml by mistake. Unstage it, keeping your edits in the working tree.
steps.fake_output: (no output: config/local.yml is unstaged; its changes are still on disk)
steps.why: 'git restore --staged' only touches the index. Plain 'git restore <file>' (no --staged) is the dangerous one: it throws away your working-tree edits, and uncommitted changes can't be recovered from the reflog.

steps.prompt: After committing, you spot a typo in the same change. Fold the fix into the last commit without changing its message (the fix is already staged).
steps.fake_output:
[fix/charge-cents 5d6e7f8] Charge in cents, not dollars
 Date: Sun Sep 28 10:02:11 2026 +0000
 1 file changed, 1 insertion(+), 1 deletion(-)
steps.explanation: The last commit was replaced by a new one (new id 5d6e7f8) containing both changes.
steps.why: Amending rewrites history: the old commit is replaced, not edited. That's fine before you push. After pushing, it forces a force-push and disrupts anyone who pulled the old one, so on shared branches make a new commit instead.

steps.prompt: Later you find a fix that belongs with an older commit, a1b2c3d. Record it as a fixup commit to be squashed in automatically later (the fix is staged).
steps.fake_output:
[fix/charge-cents 9e8d7c6] fixup! Validate currency before charging
 1 file changed, 2 insertions(+)
steps.explanation: A commit named 'fixup! ...' that marks which commit it belongs to.
steps.why: Fixup commits let you keep working and tidy up at the end: 'git rebase -i --autosquash main' moves each one next to its target and squashes it, with no manual reordering (git-tutorial-005). Reviewers get clean commits, and you never interrupt your flow to rewrite history.
